title: 6-7, rizz and rage bait: decoding the words of the year
description: Every year, the big English dictionaries each pick one Word of the Year, and lately the winners come from TikTok and AI. Each Question gives you a word, a sentence that uses it, or a dictionary definition, and asks what it means, where it came from, or who chose it. The Explanations show how lexicographers actually decide: search and usage data, a comparison against a baseline, and in Oxford's case a public vote. Covers the 2023–2025 winners, as announced.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: In 2025, a student answers "How was the test?" with "6-7" and a palms-up hand gesture. What do they mean?

options.text: Something like "so-so" or "maybe this, maybe that", or nothing at all
They scored 6 or 7 out of 10
It's a countdown to the end of the lesson
It's code for "I'll tell you later"

questions.explanation:
6-7 has no fixed meaning, and that is the point. The gesture, both palms up and moving alternately up and down like a pair of scales, suggests "so-so" or "could go either way", so some people use it that way. Just as often it means nothing and is shouted whenever a 6 or a 7 comes up. Dictionary.com called it "meaningless, ubiquitous, and nonsensical", and Skrilla, whose song started it, has said he never gave it a meaning.

A phrase with no content still does a job. Knowing when to say it, and laughing when someone else does, shows that you belong to the group. Adults who ask what it means are proving that they don't.

questions.title: Where did "6-7" come from?

options.text: A rap song, "Doot Doot (6 7)" by Skrilla
An episode of *South Park*
A maths-class joke that 6 × 7 = 42, the "answer to everything"
A dance challenge started by a TikTok brand account

questions.explanation:
The phrase comes from the chorus of Skrilla's drill track "Doot Doot (6 7)", released in December 2024. The song alone did not make it a craze. Fans set it to basketball highlight clips, a March 2025 video of a boy yelling it at a game went viral, and from June searches for it climbed.

*South Park* is the tempting wrong answer because it came late. Its season 28 premiere on 15 October 2025 built a plot around kids brainwashed by the meme, which shows the phrase was already famous enough to parody. The *Hitchhiker's Guide* joke is a coincidence: nobody connected 6-7 to 42.

images.alt: Vertical timeline of 6-7. December 2024: Skrilla releases the drill track Doot Doot (6 7). Next: fan edits pair it with LaMelo Ball, listed at 6 feet 7 inches. March 2025: a clip of a boy yelling it at a basketball game goes viral. Summer 2025: searches for 67 grow more than sixfold after June. 15 October 2025: South Park's season 28 premiere builds a plot around it. 29 October 2025, highlighted: Dictionary.com names 67 its 2025 Word of the Year.

questions.title: Why is NBA player LaMelo Ball part of the 6-7 story?

options.text: He is listed at 6 feet 7 inches tall
He wears the number 67
He once scored 67 points in a game
He recorded the song with Skrilla

questions.explanation:
LaMelo Ball is listed at 6 ft 7 in (2.01 m). Fans cut his highlight clips to the "6 7" line in Skrilla's song, and the height pun is what attached the number to basketball.

This kind of accidental link is common in meme history. The song's number meant nothing about basketball, but one good edit gave it a second context. Each new context brings the phrase to a new audience.

questions.title: Dictionary.com named "67" its 2025 Word of the Year. Which piece of evidence showed its lexicographers that the number itself was trending?

options.text: Searches for 67 grew more than sixfold after June 2025, while most other two-digit numbers showed no trend
A public vote in which 67 beat every other shortlisted word
Teachers submitted the most complaints about it
It appeared in more printed books in 2025 than any new word

questions.explanation:
Dictionary.com's editors looked at headlines, social media trends and search data. Searches for 67 rose more than sixfold after June 2025. The strongest part of the argument was the comparison: most other two-digit numbers had no meaningful trend over the same months. Without that baseline, a rise in searches for a number could be homework, sports scores or noise. With it, the rise clearly belongs to this one number.

The public vote is Oxford's method, not Dictionary.com's. Printed books lag far behind slang, which is why Word of the Year teams rely on web and search data. Dictionary.com's 2025 shortlist included *agentic*, *aura farming*, *clanker* and *tariff*. A number is an unusual winner, so the announcement included a section on what counts as a word.
questions.references: [Dictionary.com: 2025 Word of the Year](https://www.dictionary.com/articles/word-of-the-year-2025), [CBS News: Dictionary.com picks 67](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/dictionary-67-2025-word-of-the-year-meaning/)

questions.title: In 2025, many schools told students to stop saying "6-7". What was the reason?

options.text: Students shouted it, with the gesture, every time a 6 or a 7 came up, and it derailed lessons
It was a hidden code for sharing test answers
It carries an offensive meaning
The song it comes from was banned from radio

questions.explanation:
The bans were about classroom disruption. Numbers come up constantly in school: page 67, question 6, a 6 on the board in maths. Each one became a cue for a chorus of "six-seven!" and the hand gesture. Dictionary.com reported that teachers were soon trading tips online about how to stop students saying it all day long.

None of the other answers has any basis. The phrase has no hidden meaning to decode, which is exactly why a ban was the only thing that worked. You can't explain away a joke whose whole content is the interruption.

questions.title: Which longer word was shortened to give us "rizz"?
questions.description: Rizz means style, charm or attractiveness, especially the ability to attract a romantic partner.

options.text: Charisma
Rizzo, a character in *Grease*
Risqué
Rising

questions.explanation:
Rizz comes from the middle of *cha-RIS-ma*. Linguists call this clipping: making a new word by cutting down an old one. Most clippings keep the front, as in *lab* from *laboratory*, or the back, as in *phone* from *telephone*. Keeping the middle is rarer. *Flu* from *influenza* is the best-known example, and rizz joins it.

The doubled *z* follows the same spelling habit as *jazz* and *fizz*. It keeps the vowel short, so the word rhymes with *fizz* rather than *rise*.
questions.references: [Oxford University Press: Rizz crowned Oxford Word of the Year 2023](https://corp.oup.com/news/rizz-crowned-oxford-word-of-the-year-2023/), [Wikipedia: Clipping (morphology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clipping_(morphology))

questions.title: In which year did Oxford name "rizz" its Word of the Year?
questions.explanation:
Oxford picked rizz for 2023. More than 30,000 people voted in head-to-head rounds that narrowed eight shortlisted words to four finalists: *rizz*, *Swiftie*, *situationship* and *prompt*. Oxford's lexicographers then made the final call using the vote and their usage data.

The finalists are a snapshot of 2023. *Prompt*, the instruction you give an AI model, was the first sign of the AI vocabulary that took over two years later.
questions.references: [Oxford University Press: Rizz crowned Oxford Word of the Year 2023](https://corp.oup.com/news/rizz-crowned-oxford-word-of-the-year-2023/)

questions.title: Oxford's 2024 Word of the Year was first recorded in Henry David Thoreau's *Walden* (1854). Type the two-word term.
questions.description: Thoreau asked: "While England endeavors to cure the potato-rot, will not any endeavor to cure the ______, which prevails so much more widely and fatally?"
questions.explanation:
The word is *brain rot*. Thoreau was complaining that his society valued simple ideas over complex ones. That makes a 170-year-old book the first recorded use of a word most people think TikTok invented.

Oxford defines brain rot as the supposed deterioration of a person's mental state from consuming too much trivial material, "now particularly online content". More than 37,000 people voted on the 2024 shortlist, and Oxford's data showed usage up 230% between 2023 and 2024. Much of that use was self-mocking: younger people using the word about their own scrolling habits.
questions.references: [Oxford University Press: 'Brain rot' named Oxford Word of the Year 2024](https://corp.oup.com/news/brain-rot-named-oxford-word-of-the-year-2024/), [Wikipedia: Walden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walden)

questions.title: A cooking video puts ketchup on carbonara. The creator hopes that angry comments will push it to more feeds. Which term, Oxford's Word of the Year for 2025, describes it?

options.text: Rage bait
Clickbait
Aura farming
Doomscrolling

questions.explanation:
Oxford defines rage bait as online content deliberately designed to make people angry by being frustrating, provocative or offensive, usually to drive traffic or engagement. It works because a feed ranks posts by engagement, and an angry comment counts as engagement just like a happy one. The creator doesn't need anyone to agree, only to reply.

Clickbait is the near miss. It uses curiosity to get a click ("You won't believe…"), while rage bait uses outrage to get a reaction. Aura farming, one of the two words rage bait beat in the final vote, means carefully cultivating a cool image. More than 30,000 people voted, and Oxford's data showed usage of *rage bait* had tripled in 12 months.
questions.references: [Oxford University Press: Oxford Word of the Year 2025](https://corp.oup.com/word-of-the-year/)

questions.title: Cambridge Dictionary's Word of the Year for 2025 was *parasocial*. Which relationship is parasocial?

options.text: A viewer who feels they know a streamer well, although the streamer has never heard of them
Two pen pals who write every week but have never met
Coworkers who only ever talk through a chat app
Friends who met in an online game and play together every night

questions.explanation:
A parasocial relationship is one-sided. One person feels a connection, and the other doesn't know they exist. The three distractors all happen at a distance or through a screen, but in each of them both people know each other and both respond. Distance does not make a relationship parasocial. Only the missing second side does.

The sociologists Donald Horton and Richard Wohl coined the term in 1956 to describe television viewers who felt close to TV personalities. Cambridge picked it for 2025 because the idea spread from celebrities and influencers to AI chatbots, which people now treat as friends. A chatbot pushes the idea further: it replies, but nobody on the other side knows you.
questions.references: [Cambridge University Press & Assessment: 'Parasocial' is Cambridge Dictionary's Word of the Year 2025](https://www.cambridge.org/news-and-insights/parasocial-is-cambridge-dictionary-word-of-the-year-2025), [Wikipedia: Parasocial interaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasocial_interaction)

questions.title: Merriam-Webster chose *slop* as its 2025 Word of the Year. Which meaning earned it the title?

options.text: Low-quality digital content produced in quantity, usually by AI
Food scraps fed to pigs
Soft, wet mud
Overly sentimental writing

questions.explanation:
Merriam-Webster's 2025 definition is "digital content of low quality that is produced usually in quantity by means of artificial intelligence". Think fake news images, junk AI-written books and "workslop" reports that waste coworkers' time.

The distractors aren't wrong. They are older meanings of the same word. *Slop* meant soft mud in the 1700s, food waste by the 1800s, and later anything of little value. Words change meaning this way all the time: an old sense stays in the dictionary while a new one takes over everyday use. Other dictionaries agreed that year: Australia's Macquarie Dictionary chose *AI slop*, and the American Dialect Society chose *slop*.
questions.references: [Merriam-Webster: Word of the Year 2025](https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/word-of-the-year), [CBS News: "Slop" chosen as Merriam-Webster's 2025 word of the year](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/slop-merriam-webster-2025-word-of-the-year/)

questions.title: Collins picked *vibe coding* as its Word of the Year for 2025. What does it describe?

options.text: Building software by describing what you want in plain language and letting AI write the code
Programming while listening to music to stay in flow
Writing code quickly without a plan, then fixing bugs as they appear
Pair programming where one person talks and the other types

questions.explanation:
Collins defines vibe coding as using AI, prompted by natural language, to help write computer code. You describe the app in plain words, the model writes it, and you judge the result by running it.

"Writing code without a plan" is the tempting answer, because the "vibes" sound like improvising. The difference is who writes the code. Hacking without a plan is still you typing every line. In vibe coding you may not read the lines at all. Collins chose the term because its usage grew sharply after it first appeared in February 2025, in a post by Andrej Karpathy.
questions.references: [Collins: Word of the Year 2025](https://www.collinsdictionary.com/woty), [Collins Language Blog: Word of the Year 2025](https://blog.collinsdictionary.com/language-lovers/collins-word-of-the-year-2025-ai-meets-authenticity-as-society-shifts/)

questions.title: Which of these did Andrej Karpathy's February 2025 post, the one that coined *vibe coding*, actually describe?

options.text: Accepting every AI-suggested change without reading the diffs
Forgetting that the code even exists
Using it for throwaway weekend projects
Writing tests first so the AI's code can be trusted
Reviewing every line before it ships

questions.explanation:
Karpathy, a cofounder of OpenAI and former AI director at Tesla, described giving in to the vibes and forgetting that the code even exists. He said he clicked "Accept All" and no longer read the diffs, and he framed it as fine for throwaway weekend projects. Tests and line-by-line review are the opposite of what the post described.

That last condition matters for developers. Simon Willison pointed out that if you review the code an AI writes, test it and can explain how it works, you are not vibe coding any more. You are doing ordinary software development. A throwaway weekend project can survive code nobody has read. A production system can't, because someone will have to debug it and keep it secure.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Vibe coding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibe_coding), [Simon Willison: Not all AI-assisted programming is vibe coding](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Mar/19/vibe-coding/)

questions.title: Which of these were a major English dictionary's Word of the Year for 2025?

options.text: Vibe coding
Slop
Parasocial
Rage bait
Rizz
Brain rot
Hallucinate

questions.explanation:
The 2025 winners were *67* (Dictionary.com), *vibe coding* (Collins), *slop* (Merriam-Webster), *parasocial* (Cambridge) and *rage bait* (Oxford). *Rizz* won at Oxford in 2023 and *brain rot* in 2024. *Hallucinate*, in the sense of an AI model confidently making things up, won at both Cambridge and Dictionary.com in 2023.

The grid shows that the dictionaries rarely pick the same word, because they measure different things. Oxford combines a public vote with its usage data, Cambridge follows what people look up, Collins tracks its language corpus, and Dictionary.com weighs searches, headlines and social media. When different methods agree, as they did on *hallucinate* in 2023, the word really was everywhere.

images.alt: Grid of Words of the Year by dictionary and year. Oxford: rizz in 2023, brain rot in 2024, rage bait in 2025. Merriam-Webster: authentic, polarization, slop. Collins: AI, brat, vibe coding. Cambridge: hallucinate, manifest, parasocial. Dictionary.com: hallucinate, demure, 67. The 2025 column is highlighted.

questions.references: [Wikipedia: Word of the year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_of_the_year), [TIME: 2025's Words of the Year](https://time.com/7334730/word-of-the-year-2025-cambridge-collins-dictionary-oxford-merriam/)

questions.title: Which 2025 Words of the Year did their dictionaries tie to AI when announcing them?

options.text: Vibe coding (Collins)
Slop (Merriam-Webster)
Parasocial (Cambridge)
Rage bait (Oxford)
67 (Dictionary.com)

questions.explanation:
*Vibe coding* is about AI by definition, and Merriam-Webster's new sense of *slop* names AI-generated content outright. *Parasocial* is the surprise. The word dates from 1956 and television, but Cambridge said its 2025 surge came partly from people forming one-sided bonds with AI chatbots.

*Rage bait* is about human creators and engagement algorithms, not generative AI, and *67* is pure playground. So three of the five big winners are partly about AI, and one of them, *vibe coding*, is about how software gets written. Dictionaries now write about developers' daily work.
questions.references: [Collins: Word of the Year 2025](https://www.collinsdictionary.com/woty), [Merriam-Webster: Word of the Year 2025](https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/word-of-the-year), [Cambridge University Press & Assessment: 'Parasocial' is Cambridge Dictionary's Word of the Year 2025](https://www.cambridge.org/news-and-insights/parasocial-is-cambridge-dictionary-word-of-the-year-2025)

questions.title: Decode this group-chat message. Which glosses are correct?
questions.description: > ngl the new intern has zero rizz, but they vibe coded the whole dashboard over the weekend and honestly it's not slop. still weird how parasocial they are about that one tech streamer tho

options.text: *rizz*: charm or social charisma
*vibe coded*: had AI write the code from plain-language prompts
*slop*: low-quality output churned out by AI
*parasocial*: attached to someone who doesn't know they exist
*rizz*: skill at writing code
*parasocial*: good at making friends online

questions.explanation:
The sender says the intern is awkward (no rizz) but built the dashboard by prompting an AI (vibe coded), and the result is surprisingly good (not slop). The last line says the intern feels close to a streamer who has never met them (parasocial).

Both wrong glosses come from guessing a word's meaning from its setting. A message about a dashboard makes "coding skill" look like a fit for *rizz*, and "online" makes *parasocial* sound social. Slang is easy to misread this way. If the message was about coding, a reader may assume every word in it is about coding too.
questions.references: [Oxford University Press: Rizz crowned Oxford Word of the Year 2023](https://corp.oup.com/news/rizz-crowned-oxford-word-of-the-year-2023/), [Collins: Word of the Year 2025](https://www.collinsdictionary.com/woty)
